candidateRows: The maximal traditional conception of God is impossible because infinite power, knowledge, and intelligence are impossible non-extensive magnitudes.
This is Huemer's principal case against the coherence of the stipulated maximal theism and directly supplies his reason for accepting only a finite deity.

After distinguishing his objection from familiar omnipotence and foreknowledge puzzles, Huemer develops a taxonomy meant to separate possible extensive infinities from impossible quantitative infinities.

The impossibility of an infinite being does not undermine Christian theism because historically authoritative Christian formulations did not describe God as infinite in the disputed quantitative senses.
The move attempts to defeat the central incoherence charge by denying that the allegedly impossible infinity belongs to the relevant Christian conception of God.
Huemer's claim that traditional theism requires a God with impossible infinite quantitative attributes.
Swinburne accepts much of Huemer's criticism of quantitative infinity but argues that it is irrelevant to historic Christian theism and proposes addressing other coherence objections.
The coherent concept of God should be inferred from the most probable ultimate cause of the universe rather than tested as an isolated maximal definition.
It replaces Huemer's definitional starting point with an abductive methodology under which an everlasting omnipotent source is inferred from general features of reality.
Huemer's method of assessing coherence by beginning with a maximal definition containing several infinite attributes.
Swinburne points to the universe, simple comprehensible laws, conscious life, and evil as evidence relevant to identifying the most probable kind of first cause.
Omnipotence is the greatest logically possible power, and because such a being knows value without conflicting desires, perfect goodness follows from omnipotence.
The argument supplies a positive coherence relation between two defining divine attributes while excluding pseudo-actions that are logically impossible from omnipotence.
The opening discussion of whether maximal power is coherent and whether inability to perform impossible or evil acts limits God.
Swinburne defines omnipotence as power over every genuine action, argues that logical impossibilities describe no actions, and connects evaluative knowledge to unconflicted motivation.
Literal omniscience conflicts with divine freedom, so an omnipotent God must know the past and logical possibilities but cannot know future free choices.
This move preserves coherence by revising one of the motion's central divine attributes and specifying exactly which knowledge omnipotence requires or precludes.
The maximal conception under discussion treats omniscience as knowledge of every truth, including future actions and choices.
Swinburne argues that advance knowledge of one's own acts removes freedom, while effective omnipotence still requires complete knowledge of the past and logical possibility.
All-powerfulness still requires infinite power because no finite amount is greatest, while even restricted omniscience entails infinite knowledge and intelligence.
Huemer directly restores his principal infinity objection against both Swinburne's greatest-possible-power account and his restriction of knowledge about future choices.
Swinburne's claims that God need only possess the greatest possible power and that divine knowledge may exclude future free choices.
Huemer compares power with unbounded velocity, argues there is no greatest finite quantity, and maintains that mathematical, past, and present facts already constitute infinite information.
Power can coherently be maximal by covering the limited kinds of action, and Christian tradition permits a God who changes his mind rather than possessing exhaustive foreknowledge.
The response attacks both pillars of Huemer's renewed objection by offering a non-quantitative account of maximal power and historical support for limited foreknowledge.
Huemer's renewed argument that maximal power must be quantitatively infinite and that omniscience necessarily involves infinite information.
Swinburne calls the infinity inference insufficient, appeals to limits on kinds of action, and cites scriptural and theological depictions of God regretting or changing judgments.
A limit on kinds of action does not limit the power required within a kind, and restricting foreknowledge still leaves infinitely many determinate truths to know and integrate.
The move directly answers both components of Swinburne's defense and argues that neither action-kind limits nor open-future theology removes the relevant infinity.
Swinburne's appeal to finitely many kinds of action and to a theological tradition in which God may change his mind.
Huemer uses unlimited lifting and repeated lamp switching to distinguish power from action kinds, then argues that past, mathematical, and present truths still demand infinite cognition.
Treating the ability to lift any weight as infinitely partitioned power imposes an artificial mathematical conception of infinity on an ordinary unified kind of action.
This is Swinburne's direct conceptual answer to Huemer's unlimited-lifting example, challenging the inference from unrestricted ability to an impossible quantitative magnitude.
Huemer's claim that being able to lift any weight entails possessing an actually infinite quantity of strength or power.
Swinburne argues that ordinary action descriptions should be understood naturally as unified abilities and not reconstructed through a mathematician's partition into infinitely many acts.
Zeno-style spatial division is an actual infinity because infinitely many spatial points and segments genuinely exist and are traversed, even though traversal needs no infinite power.
The distinction is essential to Huemer's taxonomy of infinities because it defends actual extensive infinity while denying that every completed infinite structure requires infinite power.
Swinburne's contention that dividing an ordinary action into infinitely many parts is merely an artificial mathematical description.
Huemer distinguishes the quantitative strength example from spatial division and argues that motion really crosses infinitely many existing segments despite requiring only finite power.
A one-to-one correlation with a familiar infinite series is insufficient by itself to establish that a divided action is truly infinite.
The move directly contests whether infinite divisibility supplies the actual infinity underlying the challenge to divine power.
Huemer's claim that traversing infinitely many spatial segments constitutes an actual infinity.
After Huemer treats spatial traversal as crossing actually existing infinite segments, Swinburne disputes the inference from mathematical correspondence to genuine infinity.
God's inability to perform bodily activities does not limit omnipotence because such activities are logically incompatible with God's necessarily bodiless nature.
It supplies a general coherence defense of omnipotence by classifying apparent divine inabilities as logically impossible descriptions.
Swinburne distinguishes genuine powers from descriptions incompatible with a necessarily non-embodied God and applies the restriction to walking and marriage.
A timeless conception of God would remove conflict between divine foreknowledge and power over the future, though Swinburne rejects that conception as unintelligible.
The move identifies a major route to reconciling divine knowledge and power while explaining why the proposed defense is not adopted.
Swinburne notes that timeless divine action could align knowledge and control of the future, then explains his preference for an everlasting God in time.
A timeless God cannot change his mind because timelessness and possession of successive incompatible mental states would be contradictory attributes.
The reply presses an internal-coherence problem between a timeless divine nature and earlier claims involving changes of divine intention.
Swinburne's discussion of a timeless God alongside earlier claims that God can change his mind.
Huemer connects the proposed timeless conception to prior descriptions of divine mental change and argues that the combined attributes conflict.
The Christian incarnation appears to undermine the claim that God cannot walk or marry, since Jesus is held to be God and embodied.
The objection tests the bodilessness defense of omnipotence against a central theistic doctrine that attributes embodiment to God.
Swinburne's claim that God necessarily lacks a body and therefore cannot walk or marry.
Huemer argues that divine embodiment in Jesus supplies an apparent counterexample to the asserted logical impossibility of bodily divine actions.
The incarnation does not refute divine bodilessness because Christ has distinct divine and human natures, with bodily capacities belonging to the incarnate nature.
The response preserves the bodilessness-based coherence defense by distinguishing the divine nature from Christ's embodied human nature.
Huemer's objection that Jesus walked and could have married despite being identified as God.
Swinburne invokes the traditional two-natures doctrine to separate what applies to God as divine from what applies to the incarnate Christ.
Thomson's lamp should be analyzed through temporally extended events rather than instantaneous states, so its outcome must concern a final period of finite duration.
The move supplies Swinburne's principal metaphysical answer to a supertask intended to challenge coherent unlimited divine power.
Huemer's Thomson's-lamp challenge asking what state remains after infinitely many switches.
Swinburne denies that events occur at instants, treats instants as period boundaries, and redirects the lamp question toward an extended final period.
Thomson's lamp uses infinitely many nonzero-duration switchings within finite time and therefore does not depend on treating the final instant as an event.
The reply blocks the proposed dismissal of the supertask by showing that every component event may have positive temporal duration.
Swinburne's claim that the lamp puzzle improperly treats events as occurring at temporal instants.
Huemer grants that events require time but argues that shrinking positive intervals can contain infinitely many switchings before a finite deadline.
The lamp paradox requires neither a last switching nor zero-duration events because observers after the completed infinite sequence must still find the lamp on or off.
The argument sharpens the supertask challenge by locating the disputed state during an ordinary positive-duration interval after all switchings.
Swinburne's insistence that only a final extended period, rather than an instantaneous state, is intelligible.
Huemer describes an infinite switching schedule ending before a later period of inactivity and asks what an observer during that later period would see.
A finite interval cannot contain infinitely many periods of positive finite length, because any selected positive length permits only finitely many such periods.
The response attacks the temporal premise needed for the proposed supertask and thereby supports the coherence of the restriction on divine action.
Huemer's contention that infinitely many extended switching periods can fit inside one finite interval.
Swinburne accepts division into periods in a qualified sense but denies that a bounded hour contains infinitely many positive finite-length periods.
